strengths: Novel automated synthesis framework with symbolic verification, directly addressing data leakage in benchmarking
Comprehensive large-scale evaluation of 20+ models with detailed cost analysis and clear insights about syntax-semantics gap
Substantial benchmark resource: 19k carefully synthesized tasks with 20 curriculum levels enabling fine-grained complexity control
Strong empirical contribution: curriculum learning doubles Llama-3-8B accuracy and provides meaningful downstream improvements across multiple benchmarks
Excellent reproducibility: detailed algorithms, hyperparameter specifications, promised open release, and transparent reporting of pricing/compute costs
Insightful analysis of LLM scaling trends showing model parameter scaling brings limited gains while test-time compute demonstrates diminishing returns and escalating costs
weaknesses: Severely limited scope: entire 19k-task benchmark confined to single domain (trains classification); all tasks are single-rule learning—undermines generalizability claims about 'scalable logical reasoning' without evidence of applicability beyond this domain

Modest and underexamined downstream improvements: most gains are single-digit (MMLU +2.8%, LogicQA +0.9%, ARC +1.9%) with no statistical significance testing, and claim of broad generalization is overstated

Incomplete curriculum learning experiments: only one model trained; no ablation studies comparing curriculum-ordered vs. random task presentation; training truncated to early levels due to memory constraints; no analysis of which curriculum properties drive improvements

Lacks error analysis and diagnostic insights: no categorization of failure modes (negation errors, quantifier mistakes, etc.); binary overall score dominates despite partial score availability; limited investigation into why reasoning LLMs plateau on hard tasks

Synthetic task limitations: entirely artificial logical patterns from single domain may not reflect real-world reasoning challenges; mirror sampling in early levels likely oversimplifies tasks; no comparison with human-generated or natural logical reasoning data

Missing methodological rigor: no confidence intervals or significance testing reported; single-run results; different protocols across downstream benchmarks confound attribution; no ablation comparing curriculum strategy to simply scaling training data

strengths: Solid technical framework with clear separation of concerns (specification, synthesis, evaluation) and sound methodology grounded in ILP
Substantial and systematic benchmark: 19k tasks with fine-grained control over complexity via language specifications and configurations, enabling reproducible reasoning evaluation
Comprehensive empirical evaluation spanning 40+ models, 6 downstream benchmarks, ablations on synthesis parameters, and detailed error analysis with actionable taxonomy

Valuable empirical insights: syntax is not the bottleneck (high 80-100% syntax scores but low reasoning accuracy on hard tiers), longer reasoning correlates with failure, test-time scaling shows diminishing returns
Strong reproducibility commitment with detailed specifications (Algorithm 1, Appendix B), full hyperparameter documentation, promised code/data release, and cost transparency
Verifiable symbolic evaluation avoids reliance on LLM-as-judge and enables deterministic, interpretable task assessment
weaknesses: Scope limitations inadequately foregrounded in framing: single-rule induction only (real logic involves multiple rules and constraints), single primary domain (trains; limited OOD evidence from 500-task SLR-Homes), and synthetic data that may oversimplify real-world logical ambiguity

Overclaimed comparisons with reasoning LLMs: Llama-3.1-8B-SLR (LRL 8.7) vs Gemini-thinking (8.6) is marginal difference (~0.1 LRL), yet framed as 'surpassing' SOTA reasoning models; unfair model-size comparisons absent proper controls

Modest downstream generalization: improvements mostly 1-6% on downstream benchmarks (MMLU-Stats +17% is outlier on single task subset), with CLUTRR the most relevant at +6.6%; downstream tasks are not primarily inductive reasoning; no significance testing

Curriculum learning analysis lacks depth: Table 8 shows ordered (6.01 LRL) vs random (5.99) vs reverse (5.93) differ by ~0.08 LRL with unclear significance; no analysis of which transitions matter or why structured progression is critical when random performs nearly as well

Hard-tier performance near-zero (0-2% for most models, max 13%) suggests poor calibration (tasks too hard for learning signal) or misalignment with model capabilities; makes hard-tier evaluation uninformative

Reproducibility gaps: no error bars or confidence intervals on results, variance across runs unreported, hyperparameter choices (learning rate, batch size) not justified, sequence truncation to 6k tokens may truncate longer rules
Data leakage assurance insufficient: App. B.6 acknowledges surface similarity metrics are insufficient for semantic independence; claims of 'statistically negligible' overlap lack formal verification

Algorithm and design analysis incomplete: rejection sampling in Algorithm 1 may have high rejection rates (not analyzed), many task configuration hyperparameters (Table 4) lack principled guidance, symbolic judge only supports exact-match evaluation

Error analysis is descriptive rather than diagnostic: Appendix G identifies 5 failure modes but doesn't investigate root causes (e.g., why does GPT-5 reward-hack? Why does longer output correlate with failure in distilled models?)

Generalization claims overstate evidence: 'wide range of established benchmarks' improvement is 1-6% on most; 'domain-agnostic reasoning' tested on one OOD domain; 'systematic generalization' claims stronger than evidence supports

strengths: Well-engineered framework with fully automated, reproducible task synthesis pipeline
Comprehensive evaluation across 40+ models with extensive ablations and hyperparameter details
Deterministic symbolic evaluation via Prolog avoids LLM-judge unreliability
Solid error analysis identifying five recurring failure modes in LLM reasoning
Demonstrates curriculum learning benefits with controlled order ablations (Table 8)
Honest limitations section and detailed appendices support reproducibility
weaknesses: Severely limited scope: single domain (trains), single task type (single-rule induction), function-free Horn clauses—claims about 'logical reasoning' are overstated
Modest downstream improvements (MMLU +2.8%, GPQA +1.1%, CLUTRR +6.6%) insufficient to demonstrate genuine reasoning transfer
Mirror sampling in early levels (Levels 1-5) artificially inflates performance by making tasks trivial; design choices lack principled justification
Concerning underperformance of reasoning LLMs (o3: 45% hard, Gemini: 1% hard) inadequately explained—suggests benchmark misalignment with these models' reasoning paradigm
Limited methodological novelty: standard ILP formalism + straightforward synthesis via random sampling + known curriculum learning benefits
Training restricted to basic-medium levels due to memory constraints; unfair efficiency comparisons conflate 8B model fine-tuning with o3's reasoning architecture
Data leakage concerns despite synthetic generation (Sec B.6); acknowledged inability to guarantee complete semantic independence
Core finding—LLMs struggle with single-rule induction—is unsurprising given known reasoning limitations and provides limited new insights

strengths: Well-motivated framework addressing a genuine gap in logical reasoning benchmarks, focusing on underexplored inductive reasoning at scale with deterministic symbolic evaluation
Comprehensive empirical evaluation with extensive ablations, error analysis, and downstream generalization studies across diverse models (base LLMs and reasoning LLMs)
Fully automated and reproducible synthesis pipeline eliminating human annotation and data leakage concerns through synthetic generation
Clear practical insights: models produce syntactically valid rules but fail semantically; test-time scaling shows diminishing returns; curriculum learning substantially improves downstream reasoning
SLR-tuned Llama-3-8B matches or exceeds sophisticated reasoning models (e.g., Gemini-2.0-flash-thinking) while requiring far less compute, demonstrating practical efficiency
Excellent presentation with clear figures, well-specified algorithms, comprehensive appendices, and promised open-source release supporting reproducibility
Demonstrated curriculum learning effectiveness with transferable reasoning capabilities across established benchmarks (CLUTRR, GPQA, LogiQA, MMLU)
weaknesses: Limited domain scope: primary benchmark restricted to V-LoL trains domain; SLR-Homes provides only minimal alternative (500 tasks). Cross-domain generalization claimed but insufficiently demonstrated

Task complexity constraints: single-rule induction only (no multi-rule interactions), first-order Horn clauses without functions. While enabling control, this may underrepresent real logical reasoning challenges

Modest downstream transfer for several benchmarks (LogiQA: +0.9%, ARC: +1.9%, GPQA-Ext: +0.7%) with unclear patterns for success/failure; undermines universality claims about domain-agnostic reasoning

Incomplete analysis of curriculum learning mechanisms: shows curriculum helps but lacks mechanistic understanding of whether benefits derive from structured progression, task characteristics, or data quantity
Lack of statistical rigor: no confidence intervals, significance testing, or error bars despite stochastic sampling; makes it difficult to assess meaningful vs. noise differences
Synthetic data blindspots: purely synthetic generation may not capture natural problem distributions; no comparison with models trained on real logical reasoning problems at similar scale
Fairness of model comparisons: Llama-8B vs. Gemini-thinking conflates model size, training data, and inference strategy; cost comparisons valuable but not fully controlled
Limited RL exploration: GRPO experiments preliminary with training halted at level 7 due to 'reward collapse,' indicating potential brittleness of approach beyond SFT
Surface-level error analysis: five error types identified and quantified, but deeper investigation into why specific complexity tiers trigger particular failures is missing
